lessons.title: असणे (asṇe) — "to be," and the word your sentence ends on
lessons.gloss: to be — the verb behind आहे, the word a Marathi sentence ends on

segments.text: You have already said it: mājhaṁ nāv … āhe. Now meet the verb that form belongs to, and notice where Marathi insists on putting it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: असणे and its present आहे

segments.text: असणे — asṇe — to be.
The ending -णे (-ṇe) is the Marathi infinitive, the same ending as bolṇe "to speak." Its present tense is short, irregular, and already yours: आहे (āhe) — "am, is, are."

utterances: who: मी (I). Marathi: आहे. said: āhe.
who: तू (you, familiar). Marathi: आहेस. said: āhes.
who: तुम्ही (you, respectful). Marathi: आहात. said: āhāt.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: अ, स, णे and आ, हे

segments.text: अ is the bare vowel a; स is sa; णे is the retroflex ण ṇa carrying the -e stroke — a-sa-ṇe. आ is that first letter with an upright stroke added, the long ā. And ह + े becomes हे, ha with the same -e stroke: ā-he.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a near miss with is

segments.text: Sanskrit's word for "is" was अस्ति ásti, from the Indo-European root es-: Latin est, German ist, English is. Asṇe looks built on it, but CDIAL files it under āsate, "sits, exists" (CDIAL 1480), or ākṣeti, "abides" (CDIAL 1031). It began as staying put, not as being.
आहे is the contested piece. CDIAL weighs ásti (CDIAL 977), ābhavati, "is present" (CDIAL 1226), and āsate (CDIAL 1480), and settles on none, so treat its descent as an open question.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the sentence ends on आहे

segments.text: English slots is into the middle of a sentence: "My name is Sara." Marathi holds it back to the very end:
माझं नाव सारा आहे — mājhaṁ nāv Sārā āhe — piece by piece, "my name Sara is."
That is the rule for every Marathi verb, and āhe is where it becomes unmissable. Whatever else the sentence carries, the verb closes it.

segments.text: What is the infinitive behind āhe? (असणे, asṇe.) Where does a Marathi verb stand? (Last — the sentence closes on it.) Which everyday English word is ásti's own cousin? (Is.) Next: a verb that changes shape according to who is speaking.

lessons.title: जाणे (jāṇe) — "to go," and a present tense that gives you away
lessons.gloss: to go — and the present tense you cannot say without declaring your own gender

segments.text: Say "my name is …" once more, and hear where āhe lands. Every verb from here obeys that same rule. This one adds a second rule English has no use for.
जाणे — jāṇe — to go.
Strip the infinitive ending -णे and the stem is जा- jā-. On that stem Marathi builds the everyday present: जातो (jāto) and जाते (jāte).
Both mean "I go." Neither is more correct than the other. Which one you may say is decided by something the English sentence never mentions.
जाणे (jāṇe) is inherited from Sanskrit yāti, "goes" (CDIAL 10452).
ज is ja, and the upright stroke after it is the long ā — together जा jā. णे you met last lesson: retroflex ण with the -e stroke. Two syllables, jā-ṇe, with the tongue curled back for that second one.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the ending declares who is speaking

segments.text: English "I go" hides the speaker completely — a man and a woman say the same two words. Marathi will not let you:

utterances: speaking of: a man, of himself. Marathi: मी जातो. said: mī jāto.
speaking of: a woman, of herself. Marathi: मी जाते. said: mī jāte.
speaking of: a man, "he goes". Marathi: तो जातो. said: to jāto.
speaking of: a woman, "she goes". Marathi: ती जाते. said: tī jāte.

segments.text: The -तो / -ते swap is the whole mechanism, and it runs through every verb: bolto / bolte, yeto / yete. Hindi marks gender on its verbs too, but Marathi makes it unavoidable in the plainest sentence a beginner can build. From your first "I go," you are choosing.
Notice also what is missing: no separate word for "am." The ending carries the action, the person, and the gender at once.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "jāṇe" — to go — then the stem, "jā-"]

segments.text: What is the stem inside jāṇe? (जा-, jā-.) Which two endings split the present, and by what? (-तो / -ते, by the gender of the one the verb is about.) Can a Marathi speaker say "I go" without revealing it? (No — the choice is forced.) Next: the same ancient root, pointed the other way.

lessons.title: येणे (yeṇe) — "to come," the other half of "to go"
lessons.gloss: to come — a Sanskrit verb of going, turned around by one small prefix

segments.text: Say "I go" in your own gender: mī jāto or mī jāte. Hold that shape. The next verb is closer to it than it sounds.
येणे — yeṇe — to come.
Same infinitive ending, same machinery: stem ये- ye-, present येतो (yeto) and येते (yete), split by gender exactly as jāto / jāte was.
You met yeto in Chapter 4 as a farewell — Marathi takes its leave by saying "I come," promising the return rather than announcing the departure.
य is ya, a soft English y as in yes. Add the -e stroke above and you have ये ye — the same stroke you have been putting on णे and on the last syllable of आहे. Two syllables: ye-ṇe.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — one prefix, two directions

segments.text: Sanskrit had a verb of travelling, yā-, whose present was याति yāti "goes, travels." Middle Indo-Aryan turned that initial y- into a j-, giving Prakrit jāi — and that is Marathi जाणे (jāṇe).

Sanskrit had a second verb of going, eti, on the root i. Put a prefix on it: आ- ā- means "toward, hither," and ā- with eti is aiti, "comes near" — that is, comes. CDIAL lists Marathi येणे (yeṇe) under aiti (CDIAL 2534).

So coming is going with a prefix meaning "this way." जाणे (jāṇe) and येणे (yeṇe) grew from two different verbs of going, but येणे (yeṇe) still carries the prefix that turned one direction into the other.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "yeṇe" — to come — then the stem, "ye-"]

segments.text: What is the stem of yeṇe? (ये-, ye-.) Which Sanskrit verb does CDIAL list yeṇe under? (aiti, "comes near".) What single piece turns going into coming? (The prefix आ- ā-, "toward here.") Next: an infinitive that is also a noun, and the gender Hindi does not have.

lessons.title: खाणे (khāṇe) — "to eat," and Marathi's third gender
lessons.gloss: to eat — and an infinitive that doubles as a noun of the third gender Hindi lost

segments.text: Two infinitives so far: jāṇe, yeṇe. Say them. This third one is ordinary as a verb and quietly remarkable as a noun.
खाणे — khāṇe — to eat.
Stem खा- khā-, present खातो (khāto) and खाते (khāte) on the gendered pattern you already have.
Its root is Sanskrit खादति khādati, "chews, eats" — a solidly Indo-Aryan word with no borrowing in its history. The -d- wore away on the road to Marathi; the long ā stayed.

ख is kha — a k with a genuine puff of breath after it, the sound in English kit said hard, not the k of skit. Marathi treats that puff as a different letter, not an accent. Add the long-ā stroke and the familiar णे: khā-ṇe.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the infinitive is a neuter noun

segments.text: खाणे (khāṇe) also means "eating" — the thing, not the act of doing it. Every -णे infinitive works this way; खाणंपिणं (khāṇaṁ-piṇaṁ), "eating and drinking," is how Marathi says food and drink.
And as a noun it carries a gender — neuter, the third one. Hindi has two genders, masculine and feminine. Marathi kept all three that Sanskrit had, so words agreeing with a noun come in three shapes:
You met the neuter one five chapters ago in माझं नाव, so this table is a word you already own being shown in its other two shapes rather than a new one.
So "eating is fine" is खाणं बरं आहे — khāṇaṁ baraṁ āhe, with the neuter ending twice over and the verb, as always, last.

segments.text: What are the two things खाणे (khāṇe) means? (To eat, and eating as a noun.) How many genders does Marathi have, and how many does Hindi have? (Three against two — Marathi kept Sanskrit's neuter.) Which gender is an infinitive? (Neuter.) Next: a verb whose root you already own in a dozen English words.

lessons.title: पाहणे (pāhṇe) — "to see," and a cousin it does not have
lessons.gloss: to see — a verb CDIAL traces to pracāh, "look for", not to the root behind spectacle and spy

segments.text: Say "I eat" in your own gender — mī khāto or mī khāte. The next verb runs on the same endings, and its history comes with a warning about words that only look related.
पाहणे — pāhṇe — to see, to watch.
Stem पाह- pāh-, present पाहतो (pāhto) and पाहते (pāhte). In everyday speech you will also hear बघणे (baghṇe) for the same job; pāhṇe is the one whose history repays digging.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: पा, ह, णे

segments.text: प is pa without the puff of breath that kha had. Add the upright stroke for long ā: पा pā. Then ह ha, and the णे you now know by heart. Three light syllables, pā-ha-ṇe, usually spoken as two: pāh-ṇe.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — looking for, not looking at

segments.text: You will often read that pāhṇe comes from Sanskrit पश्यति paśyati, "sees", in its prefixed form prapaśyati, "looks out at". That root, paś-, is the Indo-European spek-, "to observe", which reached English through Latin as spectacle, inspect and spy. It is a good story, and CDIAL does not tell it.

CDIAL files Marathi pāhṇẽ, "to see, to search", under pracāh, "look for", a form it reconstructs from its descendants (CDIAL 8492), and lists pāhije, "it is needed", beside it. It builds pracāh on cāh, "see, look for, desire", the verb behind Hindi cāhnā, "to want" (CDIAL 4775), and it notes prabhāti, "appears", as a possible second source (CDIAL 8709).
So pāhṇe began as looking for something, and spectacle and spy are look-alikes, not cousins.

lessons.title: माहीत असणे (māhīt asṇe) — "to know," which Marathi says sideways
lessons.gloss: to know — built as "is known to me", so the knower is never the subject

segments.text: Say "I go" and "I come" in your own gender — jāto or jāte, yeto or yete. Five verbs obeyed that pattern. This one refuses.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: माहीत असणे and जाणणे

segments.text: माहीत असणे — māhīt asṇe — to know (everyday).
जाणणे — jāṇṇe — to know (formal, literary).
Marathi has an inherited verb for knowing and barely uses it. Everyday speech says māhīt asṇe, "to be known," built on asṇe.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: मा, ही, त

segments.text: म is ma; with the long-ā stroke, मा. Then ह + ी becomes ही, ha with the long -ī stroke, which leans forward ahead of its letter. त is ta: mā-hī-t.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: knowledge comes to you, you do not do it

segments.text: मला माहीत आहे — malā māhīt āhe — "I know."
Word by word: "to me known is." Malā is "to me," and the knower sits there, not in the subject slot. Nobody acts; a fact is in your possession, and āhe closes the line.

The same frame carries a language: मला मराठी येते — malā marāṭhī yete — "I know Marathi," literally "to me Marathi comes." Yete is feminine because the subject is मराठी, a feminine noun — not the speaker; a man says it too. The verb agrees with its subject, as always. Here the subject is not you.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a loan beside an inheritance

segments.text: माहीत is a loan: through Persian from Arabic māhiyat, "the particulars" — one of the administrative words the Deccan sultanates left in Marathi.

जाणणे is pure inheritance: Sanskrit जानाति jānāti, root jñā-, from Indo-European gnō- — the root of English know, Latin nōscere (notice, recognize) and Greek gnōsis (diagnosis). Marathi kept the cousin and gave the daily work to the loan.

segments.text: Where does Marathi put the knower? (In the dative — malā, "to me.") Which verb finishes malā māhīt āhe, and where? (आहे, last.) Why yete in malā marāṭhī yete? (The subject is मराठी, feminine — agreeing with it, not the speaker.) Which know-verb was borrowed? (माहीत, through Persian.)
